extracted.intended_audience: inventors, startup founders, and applicants preparing US (USPTO) patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on common drafting mistakes to avoid when preparing a U.S. patent application/specification and claims; focused on practical pitfalls inventors and applicants introduce that harm patentability or enforceability. Emphasizes US practice considerations that affect international prosecution as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating the Application As a Technical Paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent specifications are legal documents. They have specific drafting conventions (single-sentence claims, antecedent basis, particular transitional phrases) that conflict with technical writing norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors who write the spec like a journal article create cleanup work for the attorney and often hide the inventive concept under technical detail. Follow legal drafting conventions rather than academic/technical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Including Marketing Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "Best in class," "industry-leading," "groundbreaking," "revolutionary" - these are not patent terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing language cannot help patentability and may hurt: an opponent can quote such language to argue issues (e.g., external motivation/long‑felt need) if obviousness is contested. Marketing language has no place in a specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming Your Goal Instead of Your Mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a goal (e.g., "a system for reducing network latency") without specifying how invites attacks under §101 (abstract idea) and §112 (enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to recite the mechanism by which the result is achieved; the mechanism is what is patentable rather than a high-level goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to Disclose Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Over‑specification of one concrete choice in the prototype (material, geometry, ordering, parameter value) creates design-around opportunities for competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every concrete choice should be accompanied by disclosure of alternatives that would also work—this reduces design‑around risk and preserves broader claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistent Terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling the same thing different names across the specification (e.g., "the widget," "the device," "the component," "the unit") creates ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick one term per concept and use it everywhere to avoid ambiguity in claim interpretation and specification clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent Basis Errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The first time a concept appears in a claim, use "a" or "an." On every subsequent reference, use "the."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching terms ("a widget" then "said widget" then "the widget") is fine but inconsistent; forgetting to introduce a term properly can create §112(b) rejections. Maintain correct antecedent basis throughout claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Putting Limitations in the Preamble
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble of a claim may or may not be limiting, which makes it risky to place distinguishing features there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put your distinguishing features in the body of the claim where they are unambiguously limitations rather than relying on the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too Many or Too Few Independent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: One independent claim is too few (provides no fallback). Five or more usually waste filing fees and create internal redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balanced number of independent claims; the page recommends three as the "sweet spot"—enough fallback without unnecessary cost or redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors are those who conceived the claimed subject matter. People who only provided guidance (CEOs, advisors, contractors without conception) are not inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect inventorship can render a patent unenforceable until corrected. Determine inventorship carefully based on conception of the claimed inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring International Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions made for the U.S. filing (claim style, embodiments disclosed, prior art admissions) affect PCT and national-phase filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make U.S. filing decisions with international prosecution strategy in mind to avoid foreclosing options abroad or creating conflicts in later filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Filing Continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting the parent application issue without a pending continuation can foreclose future claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep at least one continuation pending while the patent family remains commercially relevant to preserve the ability to pursue additional claim scope later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skipping the Disclosure Statement (IDS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IDS lists prior art the applicant knows about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to file or update an IDS can lead to inequitable conduct findings that render the patent unenforceable. Timely disclose known prior art and update as needed.
